newsitem.title: USA: Confederate flag still potent U.S. political symbol.
newsitem.headline: Confederate flag still potent U.S. political symbol.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
More than 130 years after the end of the American Civil War, the battle flag of the Southern Confederacy still has the power to stir violent passions, wreck political careers and destroy lives.

In the latest flareup over the "Stars and Bars" as the Confederate military flag is called, South Carolina's Republican Gov. David Beasley finds himself enmeshed in a battle that could derail his entire career.

Controversy over the flag, seen by some southern whites as a source of intense pride but by blacks and many others as a emblem of racism and slavery, also swirls in states as far apart as Maryland and Florida.

"The flag conjures glorified images of the 'Old South', which may be comforting for some whites who see the region being transformed by economic development," said Blease Graham of the University of South Carolina.
To the National Association for the Advancement of Coloured People, the flag is an "ugly symbol of white supremacy, racism and denigration."

To Christopher Sullivan, of the Sons of Confederate Veterans in South Carolina, it symbolises "that spirit of self-defence, self-reliance and that willingness to sacrifice all and stand up for independence and principle."
But the flag has also been appropriated by extremists. It is an emblem for many far-right militias, for the Ku Klux Klan and for neo-Nazis.

Beasley's problems began when he suddenly reversed his previous position and suggested the battle flag be removed from the State Capitol building, where it has flown since 1962, to a confederate war memorial.

"Any banner we fly over the capitol, where decisions about our children's future are made, should be one that everyone can claim as their own," said Beasley, a conservative Republican closely identified with the Christian Coalition.
Beasley was shocked when several black churches in his state were burned last year and by an incident in which joy-riding Klansman shot three young blacks outside the state capital of Columbia.
Violence over the flag can cut both ways. In 1995, a young white was shot and killed in Kentucky by blacks who objected to him displaying the flag on his pickup truck.
Allan Lichtman, a historian at the American University, said enthusiasm for the confederate flag blossomed in the 1960s as a symbol of opposition to black civil rights.
"There's been a rewriting of history to depict the Confederacy as somehow noble and having nothing to do with slavery. But slavery was actually part of the Confederate constitution," he said.
Beasley's move was greeted with a political rebellion in his own Republican Party and a flood of outraged mail, much of it denouncing him as a traitor.

There was an impassioned debate in the state House of Representatives, during which one Republican called on blacks to "quit looking at the symbols, get out and get a job, quit shooting each other, quit having illegitimate babies".
The House finally passed a bill calling for a statewide referendum, in which voters would be asked whether they wanted the flag to be lowered or to stay.
"This has hurt Beasley politically, at least in the short term," said Graham.

In Maryland, the state is embroiled in a court battle with a small group of Confederate enthusiasts who display the flag on their car license plates and are refusing an official order to remove the emblem.
In Florida, two black lawmakers were firmly turned down when they recently asked for the Stars and Bars to be removed from a prominent position near the state Capitol.
"This is part of Florida state history and we're not in the business of revising Florida state history," a spokesman for the Florida secretary of state said.
One of the black lawmakers pointed out that the swastika was part of German history but few in Germany would want to see it displayed on public buildings.
